messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh Tran is a 46-year-old software engineer who came to treatment after months of insisting to himself that he should be able to manage on his own. He is married and has lived in the United States for many years, working mostly from home now, but he traces the beginning of his difficulties to combat service overseas. When he speaks about what happened, the story repeatedly breaks apart at the same place. He can describe fragments—the heat, the confusion, the sense that exposure meant danger—but he says the worst part “doesn’t come out in words.” What returns instead is a sequence that runs in his mind like a film: the sudden mechanical noise of motorcycles nearby, men shouting, the smell of fuel and sweat, and a moment of intense bodily vulnerability when he was caught without clothing and felt completely defenseless. Even in the office, when a motorbike revs in the street below, he does not just remember the event; he hears the sound again in his head as if it is happening now.

Those triggers have become woven through ordinary life. On days when a neighbor’s motorcycle starts outside the house, or when he catches a related smell in a parking garage or at a gas station, Minh feels his body tighten before he has fully registered why. The cue is immediately loaded with danger. He becomes certain that he is not safe, even at home, and if a stranger comes too close in a grocery line or on a sidewalk he experiences the approach as threatening rather than neutral. He has also become wary of unfamiliar places because he cannot quickly judge exits, distances, or who may be nearby. The triggers are potent partly because they pull up the sensory pieces of the combat memory so abruptly; the smell or sound seems to bring the scene with it, and the more often this happens, the more sensitized he has become to noticing those same cues everywhere around him.

Over time he began organizing his life to prevent that surge. He stopped watching war films, action shows, and even news coverage if there might be footage or discussion that resembled combat. He rarely goes out unless necessary, preferring routes and locations he already knows. He has also given up exercise, including jogging outdoors, because being physically exposed and out in public leaves him feeling too vulnerable and too easy to catch off guard. These choices make sense to him in the moment: if he avoids the cue, he may avoid the memory, and if he avoids the memory, he may avoid the sense that danger is present now. Yet the narrowing of his world has had consequences. His wife has become frustrated that he declines invitations and errands, and at work he has resisted coming into the office because commuting exposes him to traffic noise, strangers, and places he cannot fully scan.

The avoidance has not quieted the trauma so much as made it more dominant. Because Minh turns away from reminders and cuts off situations that might evoke the event, the memory remains largely unspoken and unprocessed, returning in the same sensory form rather than as a narrative with a beginning and end. He still experiences it as a replay, accompanied by sounds in his head from the original event, and his inability to put the worst moments into words leaves him feeling that the experience is unfinished and close. After a day of staying inside and monitoring the house, small cues begin to stand out more sharply: a faint smell, an engine outside, a person passing the front window. The more guarded he feels, the more readily these cues register as signs of immediate threat, and once they do, the memory is pulled back into the foreground again.

This loop now dominates his days. He checks who is outside, avoids new places, and remains on guard in his own home; that constant sense of threat makes him quicker to detect smells and noises linked to combat, and each detection seems to confirm that vigilance is necessary. The memories that follow make going out feel even less possible, so he retreats further, and the retreat leaves him with fewer experiences that compete with the old scene. Minh finally sought help after his wife told him that the family had begun arranging life around what he could not tolerate, and after he realized he was declining even routine in-person work meetings. What frightens him most is that a smell, a motorcycle, or a moment of exposure can still erase the distance between then and now. What he hopes, cautiously, is not to forget, but to stop feeling as though the war can enter the room at any moment.
